The mercury bellows

Sheet
9 of 56
Group
The first kind
Motion

The claim

A long airtight bellows hangs on a pivot and is joined by a pipe to a vessel of mercury. Mercury was meant to rise into the bellows and swell it until it overbalanced, tipped, and poured the mercury back into the vessel. A counterweight would then swing the empty bellows home to fill again. The scheme was printed in France, and Denis Papin took it apart in the Philosophical Transactions of 1685.

Why it stops

Papin did the sum. The mercury inside presses outward with the weight of a column about 25 inches high at best. The air outside presses inward on the boards with the weight of about 27 inches of mercury. The bellows, he wrote, must rather shut than open. Nothing rises and nothing tips.
